paragraphs.source_en: The master asked again, “You really do dare to do outrageous things. Well, did it serve the purpose?” Meitei said, “At any rate, we somehow got through it. When I looked at the local paper, it said that on the day old Makiyama, unusually enough, wore a frock coat and carried that iron fan he is never without...” The master said, “So it seems he never let go of the iron fan.” Meitei said, “Yes. When the old gentleman dies, I mean to be sure to put that iron fan into his coffin.” The master said, “In any case, both the hat and the suit were useful to the old gentleman, so that is all to the good.” Meitei said, “But there you are entirely mistaken. I thought so too, that it had all ended satisfactorily, and that was something to be grateful for. But before long a parcel arrived from the old gentleman, and I supposed he must have sent me some token of thanks. When I opened it, there was the top hat, with a letter enclosed. It said, ‘Although you were so kind as to purchase this hat for me, it is somewhat too large; I therefore ask that you take it to a hatter and have him make it smaller. I enclose by post a money order to cover the expense of shrinking it.’” The master said, “Just as expected. He really is a hopelessly literal-minded fellow.” The master seemed highly pleased to have discovered that somewhere in the world there existed a person even more obtuse than himself. Then the master asked another question: “And what happened after that?” “After that? What could I do? I had no choice but to accept it, so I wear it.” The master grinned and said, “That hat there?” The master’s wife asked with curiosity, “Is that old gentleman a baron?” “Whom do you mean?” Meitei asked. The master said, “That iron-fan uncle of yours.” “No, he is a scholar of the Chinese classics. In his youth he became obsessed with Zhu Xi learning or some such thing at the Confucian temple, and so even now, beneath the brilliant electric lights of this age, he still solemnly wears that topknot on his head. There is simply no doing anything with him.” As he spoke, he kept stroking his chin. The master said, “Still, my dear fellow, you told that woman just now that he was Baron Makiyama.” On this point alone, the master’s wife was in complete agreement with her husband. She said, “That is what you said. I heard it from the sitting room too.” “Did I say that? Ha, ha...” Meitei burst into easy laughter. “That was a lie I made up. If I truly had a baron for an uncle, I would long since have become something like a bureau chief.” He was perfectly unconcerned about his own falsehood. With an expression that seemed at once amused and worried on Meitei’s behalf, the master said, “I knew there was something rather odd about it.” The master’s wife, however, said with great admiration, “My, how well you can tell such lies with a perfectly straight face! You really are remarkably good at boasting!” Meitei said, “Compared with me, that woman is far better at it.” The master’s wife said, “You would certainly not lose to that lady.” Meitei said, “But, Madam Kushami! My boasting is nothing more than boasting, whereas that woman’s boasting is all calculated and malicious; its quality is thoroughly bad!

Wouldn’t you agree?” The master lowered his eyes and said, “Who knows?” The master’s wife, laughing, said, “It is all the same thing.”
